title: Bookkeeping Fundamentals in Canada
summary: By the end, learners can explain what bookkeeping is, list everyday records the CRA describes, describe what should appear on a business receipt, know the usual six-year keeping period (as stated by the CRA as of November 2026), and know that GST/HST record rules exist without treating this course as personal tax help.

lessons.title: What is bookkeeping?
lessons.html:
Bookkeeping is the day-to-day recording of a business’s money movements. The Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC), a federal Crown corporation, says bookkeeping means recording every business transaction in a system such as accounting software or a spreadsheet. Those transactions can include sales and other income, expenses and other payments, asset purchases, loan payments, lease payments, and investments.

BDC says good bookkeeping depends on recording that is:

  • accurate (real figures, not guesses)
  • reliable (put in the right place)
  • timely (written down promptly so details are not forgotten)
  • consistent (the same kind of entry is always recorded the same way)
  • simple (enter a transaction once when you can, so you do not create extra errors)

BDC also explains that bookkeeping is one part of accounting. Accounting is a wider professional activity used to understand a company’s finances and support decisions. In Canada, BDC notes that an accountant needs formal training and membership in a professional order, while a bookkeeper does not need that same professional membership. Many businesses still want experience and computer skills when they hire a bookkeeper.

This course teaches everyday record-keeping words and habits. It does not make you a licensed bookkeeper or accountant, and it does not say which software you must buy. The CRA says it does not issue or recommend one official record book — many paper or computer systems can work if they are clear.

If you run a small activity or help a local group, ask a professional when the numbers become more than simple lists.

lessons.title: What records should you keep?
lessons.html:
The CRA says you are required by law to keep records of all your transactions so you can support your income and expense claims. You should keep a record of your daily income and expenses. Do not send those records in with your income tax return — keep them in case the CRA asks to see them later.

The CRA does not pick one brand of book for you. You can use a book with columns and separate pages for income and expenses, or clear computerized records.

Keep separate records for each business you run. Also keep duplicate deposit slips, bank statements, and cancelled cheques.

Income records should include the date, amount, and source of the income. Record income whether you received cash, property, or services, and support entries with original documents. The CRA lists examples such as:

  • sales invoices
  • cash register tapes
  • receipts
  • bank deposit slips
  • fee statements
  • contracts

Expense records: the CRA says to always get receipts or other vouchers when you buy something for the business.

These rules are about keeping proof. This lesson does not tell you which costs you may deduct, how to fill a tax form, or how much tax you owe. That is work for you and a qualified professional, using current CRA pages.

A simple habit is to write income and expenses on the day they happen, in one place you can find again.

lessons.title: What should appear on a receipt?
lessons.html:
A receipt or voucher is proof of a purchase. The CRA says that when you buy something for your business you should always get one, and that it has to show:

  • the date of the purchase
  • the name and address of the seller or supplier
  • the name and address of the buyer
  • a full description of the goods or services
  • the vendor’s business number if they are a GST/HST registrant and the purchase price is $100 or more (before tax)

That dollar amount comes from the CRA business-records page checked in November 2026. If the page changes later, follow the live CRA wording.

If a cash-register tape does not describe the item, the CRA says you should write the description on the receipt or in your expense journal.

If a seller does not give you a receipt, the CRA says to write in your expense journal:

  • the seller’s name and address
  • the amount paid
  • the date
  • the details of the transaction

Invoice is a word you will also see. It is a bill for goods or services. Keep copies of invoices you send (sales) and invoices you pay (purchases). Together with bank records, they help tell the story of money in and money out.

Check each receipt while you are still at the counter, when it is easier to ask for a missing detail.

This is not advice about claiming a tax credit. It is about keeping clear proof.

lessons.title: How long to keep records, and where
lessons.html:
How long? The CRA says that, generally, you must keep all required records and supporting documents for six years from the end of the last tax year they relate to. For many individuals, that tax year is the calendar year. For corporations, it is the fiscal period.

The same six-year idea appears on the CRA’s GST/HST records page: usually keep records for six years from the end of the year to which they relate. The CRA may ask you to keep them longer. If you want to destroy records earlier, you must get written permission and wait for approval. Destroying required records without permission can lead to prosecution.

There are special cases (for example, some records about long-term property, late returns, objections, or a business that has ended). Those details are on the official page. This course cannot decide which special rule applies to you.

Where? The CRA says you must keep records at your place of business or your residence in Canada, unless the CRA gives written permission to keep them somewhere else. Records kept only outside Canada, even if you can open them on a screen from Canada, are not treated as records kept in Canada.

As of November 2026, those are the rules on the CRA pages cited below. Check the live pages before you destroy anything.

Keep paper records dry and in order. If you use a computer, the CRA expects electronic records to stay readable. Ask a professional if you are unsure.

lessons.title: GST/HST records, and when to get help
lessons.html:
GST and HST are sales taxes administered by the CRA. Some businesses must register, collect the tax, and file GST/HST returns. This course will not tell you whether you must register or how to file. Those decisions depend on your situation. Use the official GST/HST pages on Canada.ca or ask a qualified professional.

If GST/HST records apply to you, the CRA says you must keep records that support your returns and claims. Those records include sales and purchase invoices and other records related to your business operations and the GST/HST. If you file electronically, also keep your working copies of returns. You do not have to send receipts in with an electronic GST/HST filing, but you must keep them in case the CRA asks to see them.

Usually you must keep those records for six years from the end of the year they relate to (CRA page checked November 2026).

The course Invoices, Expenses and GST Records (Canada) looks more closely at invoices, expenses, and GST records. For now, remember:

  • write things down when they happen
  • keep proof (invoices, receipts, bank records)
  • store them safely for the period the CRA describes
  • ask for help before you guess

Help can mean your adult learning council (for a referral), a bookkeeper or accountant, or the CRA’s own pages and enquiry lines listed on Canada.ca. Guessing on a tax form is not a good substitute for official advice.
